To: Engineering Leadership
From: Platform Team
Subject: Local AI hardware expansion vs. improving utilisation

We are at a decision point about how to serve growing demand for AI workloads with the resources we have. The question is whether to purchase additional local hardware or to invest engineering effort in improving the utilisation of the equipment we already own. Both paths are viable, but they carry different implications for cost, latency, reliability, opportunity cost, and reversibility. I want to walk through those implications and offer a recommendation.

Starting with cost, buying more hardware is a straightforward capital expense. We can quote the servers, the networking, the storage, and the power and cooling overhead, and we will know the number almost immediately. What is harder to see is the total cost of ownership over the life of the equipment, including maintenance contracts, firmware updates, spare parts, and the eventual cost of disposal or resale. Utilisation work, by contrast, is mostly an operating expense. It consumes engineering time, which is our scarcest resource, and it may require some tooling or software changes that we would need to build and maintain. The upfront cash outlay is lower, but the ongoing cost is less certain because it depends on how long it takes to get the improvements into production.

Latency is where the two options diverge sharply. New hardware, if it arrives and integrates quickly, can reduce latency by adding capacity and by allowing us to place workloads closer to the compute that serves them. However, there is a real risk that we buy machines and then discover that the latency problem was not a capacity problem at all. If the bottleneck is in the application layer, in data movement, or in how we schedule jobs, then additional hardware will not help and may even add complexity. Improving utilisation, on the other hand, often attacks latency directly. By consolidating workloads, by tuning batch sizes, by improving scheduling, and by reducing idle time, we can make better use of the latency budget we already have. The risk here is that the engineering effort takes longer than we expect and that we miss a window where more capacity would have been the simpler answer.

Reliability is a subtle but important factor. More hardware means more components that can fail, more firmware to patch, and more surface area for incidents. A larger fleet is harder to monitor and harder to keep healthy, and it can mask underlying problems because there is more slack to absorb them. Utilisation improvements, if done well, can actually improve reliability by reducing the number of moving parts and by making the system easier to understand. When we run workloads more efficiently, we often simplify the operational picture, which makes it easier to spot anomalies and to recover from failures. The uncertainty is that aggressive consolidation can also concentrate risk, so we need to be careful about how far we push it.

Opportunity cost is the lens through which I see the whole decision most clearly. Every hour our engineers spend on hardware procurement, integration, and maintenance is an hour they are not spending on product features, on reliability work, or on improving the utilisation of what we already have. If we buy hardware, we are choosing to spend capital in order to free up some engineering time, but we are also committing to a new set of operational responsibilities. If we invest in utilisation, we are choosing to spend engineering time in order to preserve capital and to avoid the long tail of ownership. The opportunity cost of buying too much hardware is that we lock ourselves into a larger operational footprint than we need. The opportunity cost of not buying enough is that we may hit a capacity wall later and have to scramble.

Reversibility is the final consideration, and it is the one that most strongly shapes my recommendation. Hardware is relatively easy to reverse. We can sell or decommission servers, although we will likely take a loss on the resale value and we will have spent time on the process. Software and process changes are often more reversible than we think, but they can also be more deeply embedded than we expect. A scheduling change or a consolidation pattern can become the default way of doing things, and unwinding it can be disruptive. The key insight is that we can start with utilisation work, learn a great deal about our actual demand patterns and bottlenecks, and then make a much better-informed decision about whether hardware is truly needed.

My recommendation is to invest in improving utilisation first. We should dedicate a focused effort to understanding where our current capacity is going, to eliminating waste, and to making the most of what we own. This path is cheaper in the short term, it is more reversible, and it gives us the data we need to make a confident hardware decision later if it turns out to be necessary. I acknowledge real uncertainty here. If our growth projections are wrong and demand spikes far faster than we expect, we may regret not having bought capacity sooner. If the utilisation work proves harder than we anticipate, we may need to pivot to hardware purchases under time pressure. To manage that uncertainty, I propose we set a clear review point in six weeks, with specific metrics on utilisation, latency, and engineering effort, so that we can revisit the decision with fresh information.

I would like to open the floor for discussion.

To: Engineering Leadership
From: Platform Team
Subject: Local AI Hardware: Expand or Optimise?

We are at a decision point. The demand for local AI inference is rising, and the question before us is whether to purchase additional hardware or to improve the utilisation of the systems we already own. This is not merely a technical choice; it is a financial and strategic one, and I want to walk through the considerations before making a recommendation.

The most immediate factor is cost. New hardware requires a significant upfront capital expenditure, and that is only the beginning. There is the physical cost of power, cooling, and rack space, and the ongoing operational cost of maintenance and eventual replacement. If we buy now, we are committing a large sum against a future we can only estimate. On the other hand, improving utilisation is largely a software and process investment. It demands engineering time, which is not free, but it is a more flexible and often smaller expense. We can choose to spend that time in increments, learning and adjusting as we go, rather than making a single, large, irreversible commitment.

Latency is the next consideration. Our current systems are not consistently fast enough. When demand spikes, jobs queue, and the response time suffers. Adding hardware would increase our aggregate capacity and, if we are careful with our scheduling, could reduce that queueing. However, simply adding more machines does not guarantee lower latency if the bottleneck is actually in our software or in how we distribute work. A poorly optimised system with twice the hardware might still feel slow. Conversely, a well-tuned system can often achieve significant latency improvements without any new silicon, by eliminating waste in the processing pipeline.

Reliability is a quiet but powerful force in this decision. Our existing hardware, while aging, is known. We understand its failure modes, we have monitoring in place, and we have a rough sense of its remaining lifespan. New hardware brings the risk of unknown issues, driver incompatibilities, and a learning curve for the on-call team. It also introduces new points of failure. A larger, more complex fleet is harder to keep healthy. Improving what we have forces us to confront the fragility of our current setup, but it also gives us a chance to build more robust operational practices without the distraction of integrating unfamiliar machines.

The opportunity cost is perhaps the most important lens. Every hour our engineers spend optimising the current system is an hour they are not spending on new features, on research, or on other critical infrastructure. If we buy hardware, we free up some of that time by reducing the immediate pressure, but we spend capital that could have been used elsewhere. If we optimise, we invest that time now, with the hope of a larger return later, but we risk not moving fast enough on other fronts. The question is not just "what is the cheapest option?" but "what are we giving up by choosing one path over the other?"

Finally, we must weigh reversibility. Buying hardware is a one-way door. Once it is purchased and deployed, it is difficult and expensive to undo. We are locked into a specific capacity level and a specific cost structure for years. Improving utilisation, however, is a series of small, reversible experiments. We can try a new scheduler, measure the result, and revert if it does not help. We can adopt a more efficient model format and switch back if it causes problems. This optionality has real value in an uncertain environment.

Given all of this, my recommendation is to focus our efforts on improving utilisation first. We should set a clear, time-boxed goal to reduce our average inference latency and increase our hardware utilisation through a combination of batching, model optimisation, and better scheduling. We should treat this as a project with measurable outcomes. If, after a focused effort, we find that we are still hitting hard limits that software cannot overcome, then we can revisit the hardware question with much better data. This path is cheaper, more flexible, and keeps our options open. It acknowledges the uncertainty of our future demand while committing us to a disciplined, reversible course of action. I am confident this is the right move for now, but I am also aware that our estimates of future load are imperfect. If the demand grows faster than we expect, we may need to accelerate the hardware purchase. For the present, however, I believe the wisest investment is in the discipline of doing more with what we have.
